comments.author: adam_d_ruppe
comments.text:
What bothers me about this whole line of thought is whether you are talking or typing or whatever, there's relevant information that needs to get in the computer.... and if you're using a quality programming language and library environment, it is already pretty concise even if you type each and every letter (and if you use basic autocomplete that is trimmed even more).

(And similarly, when I'm writing messages to other people, every word there also serves a purpose and I am sometimes very specific about little style choices... but back to programming.)

Like suppose I write <button style="background: red;">Press Me</button>. OK, MAYBE the word "style" this is unnecessary, but the rest of it serves purposes, yes, even the redundant closing tag everyone loves to hate (it serves the purpose of cross-checking for nesting errors. a little redundancy is pretty universal in communication since it helps to clarify intent). If I were to say "give me a button with a red background that says 'press me'" ...... omg im not "low-level coding" because I hate typing so much but oops there's actually more letters in the English command than there is in HTML.

If you find yourself writing something over and over again, programming languages have concepts like functions and templates to bring that down. Every word you write has meaning. If you are writing boilerplate, that's also communicating something: that the canned function wasn't quite right and you need to keep the door open to some customization.

OK, there's plenty of low-quality slop out there, always has been, so this isn't true. But like...... even there it is more true than not that every line of code has specific meaning. Typing it never really was just empty busywork per se.

comments.author: mwcampbell
comments.text:
If the title is literally true, is there any good reason at all to bother with LLM-assisted programming, requiring us to learn new ways of doing things and possibly taking a step backward in the process, rather than just continuing to get better at the old way? Even the strongest benefit of LLM-assisted programming IMO, "the field will open," is offset by a possible negative.

Are there good reasons to believe that the claim in the title is not actually true?

comments.author: bediger4000
comments.text:
Does "differently difficult" entail substantially different "Best Practices" and paradigms?

Basically all of the programming things, from variable names to functions to object orientation exist so that humans, who at best have limited cognitive resources (as this article notes!) to write working, more-or-less correct programs. If LLMs take over, do easy things like "Best Practices" change? Are global variables acceptable if the LLM has an unlimited working memory instead of  5 +/- 2 items? Is "object orientation" necessary for something that doesn't have cognitive biases and respects data structure boundaries? Will memory leaks become a thing of the past when the programmer LLM never forgets? Even very simple things like descriptive variable names don't matter if the LLM can keep a mental map of variable name to meaning. I suspect iterative development like Agile will still work best, because the requirements (a.k.a. "prompting") are never complete or finished, or even accurate.

I'm really curious to see how this category of thing turns out.
